drills.q: Give the memory of a 70B model's weights at fp16, fp8/int8, and int4.
Is LLM decode memory-bound or compute-bound, and why?
drills.a: Memory-bandwidth-bound: at low batch size each decode step reads the full weight set from HBM and does roughly 1 FLOP of work per byte read, far below the compute/bandwidth ridge point -- the GPU's compute units sit idle waiting for weights.

drills.q: Name the two quantization methods discussed for weight-only PTQ and the core mechanism of each.
drills.a: GPTQ: layer-wise Hessian-based error correction. AWQ: protects salient weight channels identified via activation magnitude, using per-channel scaling.

drills.q: Explain why naive INT8 quantization of activations fails on LLMs specifically, when weight quantization doesn't have the same problem.
drills.a: Activations develop systematic outlier channels 20-100x larger than the rest in fixed feature dimensions across nearly every token (models >~6-7B params). A max-based INT8 scale either clips those outliers, losing important signal, or wastes nearly all its precision accommodating them. Weight distributions are uniform and don't have this outlier structure.

drills.q: Derive/state the SmoothQuant identity and explain why it's mathematically exact rather than an approximation.
drills.a: (X/s)(sW) = XW for any per-channel scale s -- dividing activation channels by s and multiplying the corresponding weight channels by s leaves the matmul output unchanged. It's exact because it's algebra applied before quantization, not a lossy transform of the computed function.

drills.q: Your team quantized weights to 4-bit with AWQ and saw a general chat eval improve almost not at all in loss, but throughput barely moved at batch size 64. What's the likely explanation?
drills.a: Batch size 64 is likely compute-bound (prefill/large-batch), not memory-bound. Weight-only quantization mainly reduces bytes moved from HBM, which helps memory-bound decode, but doesn't unlock faster matmul throughput since dequantization still happens before the matmul -- need weight+activation (W8A8/FP8) quantization to move the needle here.

drills.q: Rank general chat, long-context retrieval, multilingual, and math/code by how early they degrade under aggressive quantization, and explain why math/code is worst.
drills.a: Chat/summarization degrades least, then long-context/multilingual, then math/code degrades first and hardest -- math/code requires precise compounding multi-step reasoning where one early quantization-induced error invalidates the rest of the output, unlike open-ended chat.

drills.q: A long-running agentic coding session degrades in correctness the longer it runs, only after switching to INT4 KV cache. Diagnose.
drills.a: INT4 KV-cache quantization error compounds across every subsequent attention read of the cache -- errors accumulate over many decode steps, exactly the failure signature of long, reasoning-heavy sessions. Switch to INT8 or FP8 KV cache for this workload.

drills.q: You calibrated AWQ on 500 samples of English customer-support chat but deploy to a multilingual assistant. What breaks and why?
drills.a: The salient channels AWQ protects were tuned to English activation patterns; non-English (especially low-resource-language) inputs may activate different channels that weren't protected, causing degradation invisible in an English-only eval. Recalibrate on a sample matching the real multilingual traffic mix.

drills.q: A colleague says 'quantization always costs under 1% quality, it's basically free.' Give a concrete counterexample with a number.
drills.a: GPTQ 4-bit on HumanEval trails fp16 by roughly 10 points (46% vs 56.1%); some aggressive/naive quantization schemes have shown HumanEval pass-rate drops as severe as 92% on smaller (13B-class) models, since smaller models have less redundant capacity to absorb quantization error.

drills.q: Design a quantization strategy for a coding assistant with both a low-batch interactive path and a high-batch batch-review path.
drills.a: Interactive (memory-bound decode): AWQ 4-bit weight-only + INT8/FP8 KV cache, validated on a HumanEval-style held-out set, avoiding INT4 KV since code is a fragile task. Batch-review (compute-bound, large batch): add W8A8 (SmoothQuant-style) or FP8 activations to actually engage tensor-core throughput, calibrated on real code samples, not generic web text.

drills.q: When should you skip quantization entirely?
drills.a: When you have ample GPU memory headroom, the workload is latency-insensitive at your actual batch sizes, or reproducibility against a known fp16 baseline matters more than the memory savings -- the calibration and task-specific validation cost of doing quantization correctly is real and sometimes not worth paying.
